The stored record always carries every provenance field even when the value is None, rather than omitting it. A field that only exists sometimes cannot be asserted on, and AC-26 asks that EVERY record carry these -- so absence is represented as an explicit None and tested as such.
limitations: InMemoryDocumentStore is in-memory only: it holds everything in RAM and loses it when the process ends. It is a CORRECT implementation of DocumentStoreProtocol (put/get/list plus delete/count), not a durable database. A caller needing durability supplies another backend, and the protocol is what makes that a swap rather than a rewrite. It was chosen because this library forbids modifying dependency files, so a backend needing a server could not be exercised here at all.

Neither chromadb nor faiss is installed (installing them would modify dependency files, FR-2), so the adapter changes are exercised against injected fakes speaking the same API surface, exactly as they were before this task. The newly stored page range and index_fingerprint follow the identical code path, but the REAL backends remain unexecuted for these fields.

A returned ScoredDocument's source_name is the BACKEND's name, not the original file's -- core-types calls that a conformance requirement the type cannot enforce, and a retriever that cannot say which store answered has nothing to merge on. The chunk's original source_name IS preserved, but only in the stored row under _rag_source_name; it is deliberately not surfaced on the result, and a caller wanting the file name must read the stored record.

tasks.outcome: Ship an index-verifier component that proves retrieval works rather than that writes succeeded
tasks.next_action: Pre-flight. Faiss count() can include stale rows, so a count match alone is not verification.
notes: Running the example rather than only the tests surfaced the real shape of the relationship check: my first draft passed a HEALTHY expectation against a deliberately degraded store and printed 0 warnings, which is correct but not what I had labelled it. The relationship check inspects the expectation on the source/citation legs and the read rows on the membership legs, because that is all the protocol exposes. The example was rewritten to say exactly that instead of implying the index had been examined for a field query cannot return. The lesson is the one the example exists for: a printed claim that does not match the code is a bug in whichever of them is wrong.

The concrete form of the pre-flight note 'a count match alone is not verification': the AC-27 removal test deletes c-2 and puts a stale row in its place, so store.count() is still 4 and the count check PASSES. The test asserts not [f for f in verdict.fatal if f.check == COUNT] to pin that the count check was fooled, then asserts presence names c-2 anyway. If that first assertion were dropped, the test would still pass for the wrong reason and the insight would be lost.

The eventual-consistency bound is an attempt COUNT derived from wait_ms / interval_ms, not just the clock. test_the_wait_is_bounded_even_when_the_clock_never_advances feeds a frozen now() that returns 0 forever and asserts exactly 1 + ceil(wait_ms/interval_ms) attempts. A clock-driven deadline alone would have looped indefinitely on a host whose monotonic clock did not advance, and no other test would have caught it because every other test uses a clock that ticks.

self-found while re-reading _present(): the first draft had a short-circuit that returned as soon as any record of a document had been read back successfully. The loop did cover every item so it was not actually broken, but the guard invited exactly that mistake if anyone added an early break later -- it was replaced with an unconditional pass over every record plus a reasons dict, so 'absent' always carries the reason the store gave rather than a bare miss.
limitations: The source-file leg of document->chunk->source is verified from the EXPECTATION, not re-read from the index. VectorStoreProtocol.query returns results whose source_name is deliberately the backend's name (core-types calls that a conformance requirement the type cannot enforce), so the file a chunk came from is not observable through the protocol at all. The read side of relationship therefore checks only what query does expose -- chunk_id and document_id membership. A file name corrupted after the write would not be detected here; _rag_source_name (FR-48/AC-26) is written by the adapters and this component never reads it back.

Without a per-record readback, a stored vector's WIDTH cannot be inspected: VectorStoreProtocol offers count() and query(), not get(). When the store exposes no callable get (and none is injected as fetch=), dimension is established solely by the probe query being accepted at the expected width. That detects an index-level mismatch on backends that validate width -- FaissVectorStore raises StorageInputError -- but would NOT catch a single altered row in a store that accepts the probe anyway. verifier.has_readback reports which path was available, so a caller is never guessing which evidence was used.

Presence established by filtered query assumes the backend honours a flat document_id filter and that probe_k (raised to each document's own record count) returns enough rows. A backend holding more unmatched rows for that document than the expectation has could truncate the result set; in that case the count mismatch reports first, which is the earlier and more useful signal but names no record.

Warnings deliberately do NOT withhold readiness: a record with no source file or no citation location is still ready, because FR-49 asks for fatal and warning to be separated rather than for everything to fail. The consequence is that a caller reading only verdict.ok or verdict.ready ships uncitable answers -- verdict.warnings must be read too, and verdict.report() prints both.
